newsitem.title: USA: American Indians pray for end to buffalo killing.
newsitem.headline: American Indians pray for end to buffalo killing.

text.p: A group of American Indians gathered in Yellowstone National Park on Thursday to pray for an end to the killing of bison by officials trying to prevent the spread of disease.

More than 1,000 Yellowstone bison have been shot or sent to slaughterhouses this winter as they moved toward Montana grazing areas north of the huge park in search of food. That is nearly one-third of the Yellowstone bison herd, which numbered some 3,400 animals before the winter began.

"We demand that the slaughter stop," said Joseph Kicking Horse, one of several American Indians who came from reservations in South Dakota to lead the two-hour ceremony just inside the northern border of the park.

Arvol Looking Horse, a Lakota Sioux spiritual leader, lit a ceremonial pipe, held it to the earth in four directions and led prayers and songs. He wore a long feathered headdress and spoke in the Lakota language.
About 80 other opponents of the bison policy joined in the ceremony. American Indians also held prayer vigils in Helena, Montana and in Washington D.C.

The state of Montana has insisted that the bison be controlled to prevent the possible spread of disease to cattle. Some of the bison carry brucellosis, a disease that in cattle can cause spontaneous abortion.

Thick snow in the park makes it difficult for the bison to find food and they have been moving north in large numbers. The big, shaggy animals, also known as buffalo, can weigh as much as one ton and sprint at 30 miles (50 kms) per hour.
Amid controversy over the killings, Montana Gov. Marc Racicot, Montana legislators, federal agencies and President Clinton have been involved in discussions of the problem.
The American Indians who took part in the ceremony are members of the InterTribal Bison Cooperative, which has asked Yellowstone to give them live bison to start their own herds.
However, the carcasses of most of the slain bison have been donated to other native American groups.
Bison herds across the American West numbered in the millions in the last century but were hunted nearly to extinction.
